title: The Amazing Honeybee
passage: Honeybees are small insects, but they play a huge role in our world. These busy insects live in groups called colonies, and a single colony can have as many as 60,000 bees. Inside the hive, each bee has a special job: some collect food, some take care of the young bees, and one bee, the queen, lays all the eggs.

One of the most important jobs of honeybees is pollination. When a bee visits a flower to drink its sweet juice, called nectar, tiny yellow powder called pollen sticks to its body. As the bee flies to the next flower, some of this pollen falls off. This helps the flowers make seeds and fruit. Without bees, many of the foods we love — apples, almonds, cucumbers, and strawberries — would be much harder to grow.

Bees are also famous for making honey. Worker bees fly from flower to flower, collecting nectar in a special stomach. Back at the hive, they pass the nectar to other bees, who chew it and turn it into honey. It takes the nectar from about two million flowers to make just one jar of honey.

In recent years, scientists have become worried because bee numbers are falling in many countries. The main reasons are the use of strong chemicals on farms, the loss of wild flowers, and new diseases that attack bees. Some experts call this problem 'colony collapse', when large numbers of bees suddenly disappear from a hive.

There are simple ways everyone can help bees. Planting wild flowers in gardens, avoiding strong chemicals, and buying honey from local beekeepers all make a difference. As one scientist says, 'Saving the bees is not just about saving insects — it is about protecting the food on our own tables.'

title: The Story of the Olympic Games
passage: The Olympic Games are the biggest sports event in the world, watched by billions of people every four years. But the story of the Olympics began almost 3,000 years ago in ancient Greece.

The first Olympic Games took place in 776 BC in a small town called Olympia. At that time, there was only one event: a short running race of about 190 metres. The winner was a cook named Coroebus. Over the following centuries, more sports were added, including wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Only men were allowed to compete, and wars between Greek cities were paused so athletes could travel safely to the games.

The ancient games lasted for nearly 1,200 years, until they were stopped in 393 AD. For the next 1,500 years, there were no Olympic Games. Then, in 1896, a French teacher named Pierre de Coubertin brought the idea back to life. He believed that sport could bring countries together and create peace. The first modern Olympics were held in Athens, Greece, with 241 athletes from 14 countries.

Today, the Olympics are very different from the ancient games. There are summer and winter Olympics, with more than 30 sports and over 10,000 athletes. Women compete in almost every event. The games are also much bigger business, with television rights and sponsors worth billions of dollars.

However, the original spirit of the Olympics remains. The Olympic flag has five rings, which represent the five parts of the world joined together. The Olympic motto is 'Faster, Higher, Stronger'. For many athletes, simply taking part in the games is the greatest achievement of their lives.

title: Volcanoes: Fire from Below
passage: A volcano is an opening in the Earth's surface where hot, melted rock can escape from deep underground. When this melted rock, called magma, reaches the surface, it is called lava. A volcanic eruption can be one of the most powerful and frightening events in nature.

Volcanoes form in places where the Earth's outer shell is weak or broken. The Earth is covered by huge pieces of rock called tectonic plates, which move very slowly. Most volcanoes are found where these plates meet — for example, around the Pacific Ocean, in an area scientists call the 'Ring of Fire'. About 90% of the world's earthquakes also happen in this region.

Eruptions can be very different from one volcano to another. Some volcanoes, like those in Hawaii, erupt gently: lava flows slowly down the sides like a red river, and people can often watch safely from a distance. Other volcanoes erupt violently, throwing ash, rocks, and gas high into the sky. In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted so strongly that its ash cloud circled the whole planet.

Although eruptions are dangerous, volcanoes also bring benefits. The ash from eruptions makes the soil very rich, so farms near volcanoes often grow excellent crops. The heat from underground can also be used to make electricity, a clean energy source called geothermal energy. Countries like Iceland get much of their power this way.

Scientists now watch volcanoes carefully with special instruments that measure tiny movements of the ground and changes in gas. These warnings have saved thousands of lives by giving people time to leave dangerous areas. Still, as one volcanologist says, 'We can watch a volcano, but we can never fully control it.'

title: AI in Medicine: The Doctor's New Assistant
passage: Artificial intelligence is changing many industries, but few areas show its promise — and its risks — as clearly as medicine. From reading X-ray images to predicting disease, AI systems are now working alongside doctors in hospitals around the world.

One of the most successful uses of AI is in medical imaging. A trained radiologist needs years of study to spot a small tumour in a scan, but AI models can now do this task in seconds, often with equal or better accuracy. In 2023, a large study found that an AI system detected breast cancer in mammograms with fewer missed cases than human doctors working alone. Importantly, the best results came not from AI alone, but from doctors and AI working together.

AI is also helping with early warning. By analysing patterns in millions of patient records, machine learning systems can predict which patients are likely to develop conditions such as heart disease or diabetes years before symptoms appear. This gives doctors a chance to act early, when treatment is simpler and cheaper. In some hospitals, AI monitors patients in intensive care, alerting nurses the moment a patient's condition starts to worsen.

However, the technology raises serious questions. AI systems learn from data, and if that data comes mostly from one group of people, the system may work poorly for others. Researchers have found examples where diagnostic AI performed worse for patients with darker skin, simply because they were underrepresented in the training data. Privacy is another concern: medical records are among the most sensitive data a person has.

Regulation is struggling to keep up. Unlike a new drug, which must pass years of clinical trials, many AI medical tools reach hospitals with limited testing. Experts argue that AI should be treated as an assistant, not a replacement. As one leading doctor explains, 'AI can process more data than any human, but it cannot sit beside a frightened patient and understand what they are going through.'

title: The Remote Work Revolution
passage: In 2019, working from home was a rare privilege, enjoyed by only a small minority of office workers. Then the pandemic forced millions of people to do their jobs from kitchen tables and spare bedrooms. Five years later, remote and hybrid work have become a permanent part of working life in many countries — and researchers are still debating whether this change is good or bad.

Supporters point to clear benefits. Studies consistently show that remote workers save one to two hours a day by not commuting, time they often spend on sleep, exercise, or family. Companies report lower office costs, and many employees say they are more productive at home, with fewer interruptions from meetings and office noise. The environment benefits too: fewer commuters means less traffic and lower carbon emissions.

Critics, however, warn about hidden costs. Young workers, they argue, miss out on the informal learning that happens by watching experienced colleagues. Building trust and team spirit is harder over video calls, and some managers complain that creativity suffers when people rarely meet in person. There are also concerns about isolation: surveys show that a significant number of remote workers feel lonely, especially those living alone.

Perhaps the most interesting finding is that the effects depend greatly on the type of work. Tasks that require deep focus, such as writing or programming, are often done better at home. But work that depends on quick, unplanned conversations — brainstorming new ideas or solving sudden problems — still seems to work better face to face. This may explain why most companies have settled on hybrid models, asking employees to come to the office two or three days a week.

The debate is far from over, but one thing is clear: the old idea that serious work can only happen in an office is gone forever. As one management researcher puts it, 'The question is no longer where we work, but how we work well wherever we are.'

title: Coral Reefs: Cities Under the Sea
passage: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, yet they support around 25% of all marine life. These underwater structures, built over thousands of years by tiny animals called coral polyps, are among the most diverse ecosystems on Earth — often described as the rainforests of the sea.

Reefs are also vital for people. More than 500 million people depend on reefs for food, income, or coastal protection. The complex structure of a reef acts as a natural barrier, absorbing up to 97% of a wave's energy before it reaches the shore. In countries like the Philippines and Indonesia, reef tourism brings in billions of dollars each year.

Despite their importance, reefs are in serious trouble. When ocean water becomes too warm, corals expel the tiny algae living inside them — the algae that give corals their colour and most of their food. Without these algae, the corals turn white, a process called bleaching. If the water stays warm for too long, the corals die. Mass bleaching events, once rare, now happen every few years on reefs worldwide.

Pollution and overfishing add to the damage. Chemicals from farms wash into the sea and feed harmful algae that smother young corals. In some regions, destructive fishing methods physically break the reef structure. Scientists estimate that the world has already lost about half of its shallow-water corals in the last 30 years.

There is still hope. Researchers have discovered that some corals are naturally more resistant to heat, and they are breeding these 'super corals' for reef restoration projects. Marine protected areas, where fishing is limited, have also shown remarkable recovery. As one marine biologist says, 'Reefs have survived for millions of years. If we give them a chance, they can come back — but the window is closing.'

title: The Power of Music on the Human Mind
passage: Music is found in every known human culture, from ancient drum ceremonies to modern streaming playlists. But why does a simple sequence of sounds have such a powerful effect on our emotions, our memories, and even our health?

Part of the answer lies in the brain's reward system. When we listen to music we enjoy, the brain releases dopamine, the same chemical involved in the pleasure of eating good food. Interestingly, the strongest response often comes not during the favourite part of a song, but just before it — the brain enjoys predicting what comes next. This may explain why we can listen to the same song hundreds of times without getting bored.

Music is also closely linked to memory. The part of the brain that processes music sits near the areas responsible for autobiographical memories, which is why a song from our teenage years can instantly bring back forgotten moments. Doctors have used this connection to help patients with Alzheimer's disease: even when other memories fade, many patients can still sing songs they learned decades ago.

Beyond emotion and memory, music affects the body directly. Studies show that listening to calm music can lower heart rate and reduce stress hormones, while rhythmic music can improve movement in patients recovering from strokes. Some surgeons even play music in the operating room, reporting that it helps them focus during long, difficult procedures.

Despite centuries of music-making, scientists admit that many questions remain unanswered. Why do some people love heavy metal while others find it unbearable? Why does a sad song sometimes make us feel better? As one researcher notes, 'We understand the physics of sound perfectly, but the mystery of why music moves us is still largely unsolved.'
